questions.prompt: Per this course's definition, what does data lineage actually record?
options: The recorded path data takes from its origin, through every transformation, to every place it's used
A list of every table in a database, regardless of whether data moves between them
The current schema of a table, including column names and data types
A security audit log of who accessed a dataset and when
The business glossary definition of a data element, without reference to its movement
A performance benchmark of how long a query takes to run
questions.explain: Lineage is specifically the recorded path data takes from origin through every transformation to every place it's used — the package-tracking analogy from Lesson 1: a map of the whole journey, recorded well enough that someone other than the original builder can retrace it.
questions.distractorExplain: Option E describes what the business glossary from the prior Metadata Management course gives you — a definition and identity for a term. Lineage is different: it's not about what a term means, but about the recorded path data takes as it moves and transforms, which is exactly why Lesson 2 describes the two courses as extending from identity to movement rather than overlapping.

questions.prompt: stg.Orders_Clean has a CustomerNotes column, and table-level lineage shows one plain arrow feeding dw.FactSales with no column detail. A developer wants to change CustomerNotes's data type and, based on that arrow alone, assumes the change is risky. Column-level lineage then shows CustomerNotes isn't referenced in any column mapping into dw.FactSales. What should the developer conclude, and why?
options: The table-level arrow overstated the risk — column-level lineage shows the change is actually safe, since CustomerNotes isn't used in any mapping into FactSales
The column-level lineage result must be wrong, since the table-level arrow already proved every column in the source is used downstream
Both results agree, since a table-level arrow always implies every column feeding it is also used individually downstream
The developer should still treat the change as unsafe, since the table-level arrow already confirmed a dependency exists
questions.explain: A table-level arrow implies every column in the source might matter to the target, which is almost never actually true. Column-level lineage checks the real column mappings directly and shows CustomerNotes isn't one of them — exactly Lesson 4's point that a table-level arrow alone can give a false sense of having answered an impact question when it hasn't.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in the package-tracking analogy from Lesson 1, each scan event — an extraction, a transformation, a load — corresponds to one recorded step in a data lineage path called a ________.
questions.explain: A hop is one recorded step in a lineage path, equivalent to a single package scan at a sorting facility — if a number looks wrong, you walk the hops backward until you find where it diverged from what it should be.

questions.prompt: Select every one of the four business reasons this course gives for investing in data lineage, per Lesson 2.
options: Trust — being able to answer "where did this number actually come from" with a traceable chain
Impact analysis — knowing what else depends on a column before changing it
Root cause analysis — walking backward from a broken report to the exact hop where things diverged
Regulatory and audit requirements — demonstrating how a reported figure was calculated
Reducing the storage cost of a data warehouse by eliminating duplicate tables
questions.explain: Lesson 2 names exactly four reasons: trust, impact analysis, root cause analysis, and regulatory/audit requirements. Storage cost reduction is never one of them — lineage is about traceability, not storage efficiency.

questions.prompt: Match each lineage-capture approach or standard to what it actually is, per Lesson 5.
right: Reads actual transformation code without running it, to automatically derive lineage
An open specification for describing lineage events in a tool-independent format
Someone writes down, by hand, what feeds what
Observes what actually happens when a pipeline runs, to record real executed behavior
questions.explain: Manual documentation is written by hand. Static parsing reads source code without running it. Runtime capture observes what actually happened during execution. OpenLineage isn't a capture method at all — it's an open specification so different tools can describe lineage events in a shared, portable format.

questions.prompt: Put these hops in the order Lesson 1 describes a single number actually traveling, from a source system to a dashboard.
items: An order gets placed in a source system
A nightly job extracts the order into a landing zone
A transformation step in staging cleans and reshapes the data
The cleaned data is loaded into a warehouse table
The warehouse data is aggregated into a semantic model
The semantic model's value is displayed on a dashboard
questions.explain: This is Lesson 1's own worked chain: a number is entered at a source, extracted, transformed in staging, loaded into a warehouse, aggregated into a semantic model, and finally rendered on a dashboard — each arrow being one hop, the lineage equivalent of a package scan.

questions.prompt: What does Change Data Capture (CDC) extraction actually do?
options: Reads a database's own transaction log to capture every insert, update, and delete as a discrete, ordered event
Pulls every row from a table, every time it runs, regardless of what changed
Pulls only rows new or changed since the last run, filtered on a modified_date column
Makes paginated calls against a vendor's API, bounded by a date range or cursor token
Compares two full extracts and infers changes after the fact by diffing them
Permanently deletes source rows once they've been successfully extracted
questions.explain: CDC reads the database's own transaction log, capturing every insert, update, and delete as a discrete, ordered event — the richest of the four extraction methods, since it preserves a row's full history of changes rather than just its current state.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C describes incremental extraction, not CDC. Incremental extraction relies on a modified_date-style column and only sees a row's current state, which means it can't see a delete at all, since a deleted row has no modified_date left to filter on. CDC instead reads the transaction log directly, so it captures deletes as their own discrete event.

questions.prompt: A team is designing a new pipeline and cares about lineage visibility. Querying their landing zone shows raw, untransformed vendor data sitting in queryable tables before any cleaning happens. Per Lesson 7, is this pipeline ETL or ELT, and why does that matter for lineage?
options: It's ELT — raw data lands before transformation, and a tool like dbt can often parse the transformation code itself to generate lineage automatically, instead of needing separately documented job definitions
It's ETL — raw data landing before transformation is exactly what defines ETL, and lineage there is captured automatically by the warehouse
It's ELT, but this actually makes lineage harder to capture, since ELT never preserves raw data at all
It's ETL, and lineage in ETL is always a byproduct of the transformation code, the same as in ELT
questions.explain: Raw, untransformed data landing before any transformation is exactly ELT's defining trait. Lineage in ELT is often a natural byproduct of the transformation code itself — a dbt model's references to upstream models declare lineage edges directly in SQL, which a tool can parse automatically, unlike ETL's lineage, which usually lives in an orchestration tool's job definitions and has to be reconstructed by hand if undocumented.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the medallion (bronze/silver/gold) pattern and warehouse lineage, per Lesson 8.
options: Bronze is raw data, exactly as extracted, untouched
Silver is cleaned and conformed, but still roughly one row per source record
Gold is business-ready data, aggregated and joined across sources for a specific use
A regular view recomputes from its underlying tables every time it's queried, so it has no lineage lag
A materialized table always reflects the current moment, the same as a view, with no refresh lag
questions.explain: Bronze, silver, and gold are exactly as Lesson 8 defines them. A view recomputes on every read, so it has no lag. A materialized table is the opposite of lag-free — it reflects whatever its last refresh pulled, which might be hours or a day stale, not the current moment.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a semantic model in ________ mode queries the warehouse live on every report interaction, so it's always current but inherits the warehouse's own freshness — unlike Import mode, which copies data at refresh time and is frozen until the next refresh.
questions.explain: DirectQuery queries the warehouse live on every interaction, so it's always current, but any staleness or lag already present upstream in the warehouse propagates straight through to the report, unfiltered — unlike Import mode's own, separate freshness lag.

questions.prompt: Match each extraction method to what it actually preserves about lineage, per Lesson 6.
right: Lineage depends entirely on what the vendor's endpoint itself tracks, such as a last-modified field
Pulls every row every time; lineage is only "this whole table, as of this run"
Captures a row's full history of changes, including deletes, as discrete ordered events
Pulls only rows new or changed since the last run, usually filtered on a modified-date column
questions.explain: Full extract gives you only the current whole-table snapshot. Incremental extract filters on a modified-date column. CDC reads the transaction log for a full ordered change history. An API pull's lineage is bounded entirely by whatever the vendor's own endpoint happens to expose.

questions.prompt: In Power BI's lineage view, what does selecting an artifact's double-arrow icon (rather than the card itself) do?
options: Highlights that artifact's full upstream and downstream chain in color, and dims everything else on the canvas
Opens a side panel showing that artifact's sensitivity label, endorsement, and refresh time
Deletes that artifact's lineage relationships from the workspace
Promotes that artifact to Certified status automatically
questions.explain: Selecting the double-arrow icon isolates one artifact's chain — upstream and downstream — highlighting it and dimming everything unrelated, per Lesson 10. Selecting the card itself (not the icon) is what opens the metadata side panel instead.

questions.prompt: Put these hops in the order data actually flows, from a source system to an executive dashboard, per Chapter 2.
items: An OLTP database or SaaS API is extracted into a landing zone (bronze)
Bronze data is cleaned and conformed into silver
Silver data is aggregated and joined into a gold-layer fact table in the warehouse
A semantic model imports or DirectQueries the gold-layer table and defines measures
A Power BI report is built on top of the semantic model
An executive dashboard surfaces the report's visual as the final, visible tile
questions.explain: This is the full Chapter 2 chain: extraction into bronze, cleaning into silver, aggregation into a gold fact table, a semantic model layer with its own measures, a report built on that model, and finally a dashboard — the tip of the chain most of its viewers never see past.

questions.prompt: In the chain SourceTable -> StagingView -> FactTable -> Report, is StagingView upstream or downstream?
options: Both — StagingView is downstream of SourceTable and upstream of FactTable, at the same time
Only downstream — once something is downstream of one node, it can never be upstream of anything else
Only upstream — StagingView is always the starting reference point for the whole chain
Neither — upstream and downstream only apply to the very first and very last node in a chain
questions.explain: Upstream and downstream are relative to a chosen reference point, not absolute. StagingView is simultaneously downstream of SourceTable (which feeds it) and upstream of FactTable (which it feeds) — exactly Lesson 12's point about why you always have to ask "upstream of what?"

questions.prompt: A calculated field is defined as Revenue = Price * Quantity - Discount. Select every true statement about this, per Lesson 13.
options: The multiplication Price * Quantity is mechanical, but which Discount field to use and whether Revenue includes tax are business rules, not arithmetic
The business rules behind this formula could change silently, with no column renamed, type changed, or location moved
Lineage documentation that only tracks structure (that StagingView feeds FactTable) and ignores embedded business rules will catch this kind of silent change
Checking that this transformation's logic actually matches its glossary definition of "Revenue" is a legitimate part of documenting lineage well
A rename of CustomerID to Customer_Key is harder to detect than a silent change to this Discount logic
questions.explain: The arithmetic is mechanical, but the Discount and tax decisions are business rules buried inside it, and those rules can change invisibly since nothing structural (name, type, location) has to move for that to happen. Structure-only documentation will specifically miss this kind of change, not catch it — the opposite of option C. And it's the rename that's the easy, visible change to detect; a silent logic change is the harder one, the reverse of option E.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Metadata Management & Business Glossary's concept of a ________ Data Element is what tells impact analysis that a change touching even one downstream consumer can matter more than a change touching twenty non-critical ones.
questions.explain: A Critical Data Element (CDE) is a data element whose errors have outsized consequences for regulatory reporting, financial statements, or major decisions. Per Lesson 14, a change that ripples through twenty minor tables is lower-stakes than one that touches a single CDE feeding a regulatory report.

questions.prompt: Match each stage of a change impact assessment to what it actually does, per Lesson 15.
right: The change is described precisely — what's changing, in what dataset, field, or transformation
The downstream walk is performed and documented, not just done in someone's head
Findings are scored, typically high/medium/low, based on what was found downstream
Someone with authority approves, and owners of affected consumers are notified before it ships
questions.explain: The four stages run in order: Propose states the change precisely, Trace lineage performs and documents the downstream walk, Classify risk scores what was found, and Sign off and communicate gets approval and notifies affected owners before anything ships.

questions.prompt: ExecutiveRevenueDashboard shows revenue 8% lower than finance's own numbers. Walking upstream: RevenueFact matches StagingView (correct), StagingView matches SourceTable (correct), but SourceTable is missing rows from the 14th (wrong). Where does the fix actually belong, and why?
options: At SourceTable, because that's the specific hop where correct data became incorrect — even though the dashboard is where the problem was first noticed
At ExecutiveRevenueDashboard, because that's where the symptom was first noticed
At RevenueFact, because it's the hop closest to the dashboard
At StagingView, because it's the midpoint of the chain
questions.explain: Root cause analysis walks upstream until it finds the hop where data was correct just before and wrong just after. Here that hop is SourceTable itself — a source system that failed to send a batch of orders. The dashboard is only where the symptom was noticed, not where the break actually happened.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the impact-analysis process in the correct order, per Lesson 14.
items: Identify the change point — the exact dataset, column, or transformation about to change
Traverse downstream — walk every outgoing dependency from that point, recursively, until reaching the leaves
Classify what you find — not every consumer is equally affected, and CDEs matter more than non-critical ones
questions.explain: Impact analysis starts by pinning down exactly what's changing, then walks every outgoing dependency recursively until it reaches leaves like reports and dashboards, and only then classifies what was found — since not every downstream consumer carries the same stakes.

questions.prompt: A team's lineage documentation lists every dataset and every dependency between them, but no entry says who maintains each dataset. What does this documentation fail to support, per Lesson 17?
options: It tells you what is affected by a change but not who to tell — defeating half the point of a change impact assessment
Nothing — ownership is optional and has no effect on impact analysis or root cause analysis
It means the nodes and edges themselves must be incorrect
It only matters for business lineage, not technical lineage
questions.explain: Lineage documentation should capture nodes, edges, and ownership. Without ownership, a change impact assessment can find every affected consumer but has no person to actually notify — a dead end that undermines the sign-off and communication stage even when nodes and edges are perfectly documented.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about automated versus manual lineage, per Lesson 19.
options: Automated lineage stays current almost by definition, since re-running the scan after a code change updates the graph with it
Manual lineage's biggest weakness is durability — it's accurate the day it's drawn and nothing automatically keeps it that way
Automated lineage can see a manual Excel export someone emails to a stakeholder, since that's still part of the pipeline
Automated lineage's biggest blind spot is exactly what it can't see — anything not expressed in code or logs it can parse
Most mature lineage practices pick exactly one of the two approaches rather than mixing them
questions.explain: Automated lineage regenerates from the real pipeline on every scan, while manual lineage decays the moment nobody remembers to update it. Automated scanning specifically cannot see a manual Excel export or any step outside parseable code — that's its real blind spot, not something it can see. Most mature practices use a hybrid of both, not exactly one.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: almost every lineage diagram follows the same visual grammar — boxes represent datasets, and ________ represent the direction data flows, always pointing from upstream to downstream.
questions.explain: Per Lesson 18's visual conventions, boxes are datasets, and arrows show the direction of flow from upstream to downstream, with the arrowhead itself telling you which way the data moves.

questions.prompt: Match each lineage tool or standard to what it actually is, per Lesson 20.
right: An open specification for structuring and sharing lineage metadata between different tools, not a product you install
Scans supported data sources across an organization's data estate and automatically builds a lineage map
An open-source metadata and governance framework originally built for the Hadoop ecosystem
Generated automatically from every ref() call between models, with no separate lineage tool required
questions.explain: Purview scans an organization's data estate and builds lineage centrally. Apache Atlas is an open-source metadata/governance framework from the Hadoop ecosystem. dbt generates its own lineage graph automatically from ref() calls. OpenLineage isn't a product at all — it's an open specification other tools can emit lineage in.

questions.prompt: A lineage graph still shows a source system that was decommissioned eight months ago. What does Lesson 21 call this, and what practice specifically catches it?
options: A dead node — caught by periodically auditing the graph for datasets and reports that no longer actually exist
Lineage drift — caught only by re-scanning automated lineage, with no other practice able to catch it
A fragile dependency — caught by assigning ownership of each individual node
A matching key — caught by reviewing lineage on every change ticket
questions.explain: A documented dataset or report that no longer actually exists is a dead node, per Lesson 21. The specific practice that catches it is a periodic audit for dead nodes — re-scanning automated lineage alone wouldn't necessarily remove a decommissioned system that no longer appears in any code at all.

questions.prompt: A team wants lineage documentation that can auto-generate and stay current without manual upkeep, but accepts it may not capture undocumented manual steps. Which location from Lesson 17 are they actually choosing, and what's the tradeoff?
options: A dedicated lineage tool — it can auto-generate and stay current, but requires tooling investment and may not capture undocumented manual steps
A wiki page or shared doc — easy to write and flexible, but it requires no tooling investment at all
A metadata repository — centralized and searchable, and it always captures every undocumented manual step automatically
Any of the three locations equally, since they all carry identical tradeoffs
questions.explain: Per Lesson 17's comparison, a dedicated lineage tool can auto-generate and stay current, which is exactly the strength described here — but its listed weakness is requiring tooling investment and potentially missing undocumented manual steps, unlike a wiki page (low cost, no auto-generation) or a metadata repository (centralized, but only as good as what's entered into it).

questions.prompt: In the Brightleaf Outfitters revenue case study, a table-level arrow (stg.Transactions_Clean -> dw.FactSales) alone would not have found the $200K discrepancy. What did finding it actually require?
options: Checking the actual filter condition at the column level — TransactionType = 'Voided' — which had started also catching legitimate after-hours sales due to a POS-side labeling change
Rebuilding the entire pipeline from scratch, since the table-level lineage record was fundamentally wrong
Asking the original pipeline builder, since no amount of lineage tracing could have found it
Comparing POS daily totals to the report for every single day of the year until a mismatch happened to appear
questions.explain: The analyst found the bug by using column-level lineage to check the actual filter condition in the transformation step, discovering that TransactionType = 'Voided' had started excluding legitimate after-hours sales along with true voids — a table-level arrow alone would have shown only that the two tables were connected, not what the connection actually did.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the Caldwell & Finch customer-data case study, per Lesson 23.
options: Each of the three source systems' lineage was fine within itself — the problem only appeared when a downstream unified view tried to merge all three
The unified customer view matched records by email address, which drifted due to inconsistent formatting across systems
The lasting fix was purely a technical formatting patch, with no change to which system is authoritative
The three systems never had an agreed source of record for which system's customer identifier is authoritative
The duplicate-record problem and the creeping customer-count metric turned out to share one root cause
questions.explain: Each system was internally consistent; the mismatch only surfaced at the merge. The merge matched on email, which drifted in formatting across systems. The lasting fix wasn't just a formatting patch — it was designating the CRM's CRM_ID as the authoritative source of record, since no system had been designated that way before. And both symptoms — duplicate sends and the creeping customer count — traced back to the same underlying matching bug.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in the Northfield Pantry practice lab, POS.Sales.SaleDate and Stores.RegionMap.Region both matter to the pipeline but are never part of the revenue calculation itself — each is instead a ________, a column used to determine which output row a value belongs to.
questions.explain: SaleDate and Region are grouping keys — they decide which summary row a value lands in (which day, which region) without being part of the actual arithmetic that computes TotalRevenue, exactly the distinction Exercise 1 draws out.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 5 scenario to its actual root cause.
right: A re-issued StoreID that RegionMap still had the old value for, silently dropping that store from the join
A relabeled TransactionType field that started excluding legitimate after-hours sales along with true voids
No agreed source-of-record identifier, so an informal email match drifted wrong across three systems
questions.explain: Brightleaf's shortfall traced back to a POS-side TransactionType relabeling. Caldwell & Finch's duplicates traced back to merging three systems with no agreed source of record, matched informally on email. Northfield's $0 Midwest week traced back to a re-issued StoreID that the RegionMap join never caught up with.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of diagnosing WeeklyRegionalReport's $0 Midwest week in the correct order, per the Northfield Pantry lab's Exercise 3.
items: Notice that DailyStoreSummary already shows normal revenue for the Midwest stores on those days
Conclude the break must be downstream of DailyStoreSummary, not upstream of it
Check the join between DailyStoreSummary and Stores.RegionMap on StoreID
Find that one Midwest store's StoreID was re-issued and RegionMap still has the old value, so the join silently drops its rows
questions.explain: Since DailyStoreSummary already had the correct numbers, the break had to be downstream of that point rather than upstream of it — pointing straight at the RegionMap join, where a re-issued StoreID turned out to be silently dropping that store's rows from the Midwest total.
